the molecular mechanisms of cell migration on extracellular matrix (ECM).
the molecular mechanisms of force-dependent cell–matrix adhesion.
understanding how the cellular response to mechanical force regulates the formation and function of adhesion sites.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RPTPalpha is required for the formation of focal complexes, and that this is mediated through Fyn activation.
RPTPalpha is a novel component of a force-dependent signal transducing pathway that is essential for focal adhesion assembly on vitronectin and fibronectin.

RPTP-α is a key regulator of integrin-mediated cell adhesion, and that its activity is required for the assembly of focal adhesions on both fibronactin and vitronactin, as well as for the force-dependent reinforcement of adhesion sites.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
RPTP-α is a key player in regulating the assembly of adhesion complexes in response to mechanical forces.
RPTP-α is an early transducer of force on αv-integrin–ECM interactions, and that this is mediated by Fyn activation.
RPTP-α plays an important role in the early events of cell adhesion to ECM.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RPTP-α, which is known to be involved in many signaling pathways, also acts as a transducing receptor that links integrin signaling with cytoskeletal dynamics in the cell.
RPTP-α is a key component in the force-dependent activation of Src-family kinases and that this is a critical step in the assembly of integrin adhesion sites during cell spreading.
RPTP-α, an enzyme that dephosphorylates tyrosine residues, is an important component in the signaling pathway that transduces mechanical force to the inside of a cell.
